videos.title: Why California’s $33B Bullet Train Is Now a $231B Problem | WSJ
videos.description:
California’s high-speed rail project promised to connect Los Angeles and San Francisco with trains traveling up to 220 mph. Eighteen years after voters approved Proposition 1A, the ambitious transportation project lacks any finished track and faces an uncertain future. Costs are now projected to reach $126 billion with land acquisition and regulatory hurdles still putting America’s largest active infrastructure endeavor in jeopardy.

WSJ travels to construction sites, analyzes satellite images and reviews legal filings to explain what comes next for the multi-billion-dollar project.

videos.title: Ajay Banga on AI, Jobs & Opportunity | Global AI & Digital Summit
videos.description:
At the Global AI & Digital Summit in Seoul, World Bank Group President Ajay Banga discusses the future of development, the role of digital technology, and the opportunities and challenges presented by artificial intelligence.

He discusses the importance of getting the fundamentals of digital development right, including electricity, connectivity, affordability and digital public infrastructure, and shares examples of how locally relevant AI tools are being used in agriculture, health and education.

He also explores “small AI” and the opportunity for job creation and productivity through AI, particularly for developing countries, as well as the World Bank Group’s role in helping move promising solutions from pilots to delivery at scale.

Watch the conversation to hear his vision for using technology to drive jobs, productivity, dignity, and opportunity.

Learn more: https://live.worldbank.org/en/event/2026/global-ai-digital-summit-small-ai?cid=ECR_YT_Worldbank_EN_EXT 

ABOUT 🌐 The World Bank Group is one of the world’s largest sources of funding and knowledge for low-income countries. Its five institutions share a commitment to reducing poverty, increasing shared prosperity, and promoting sustainable development on a livable planet. http://www.worldbank.org

videos.title: Closing the Gap: The Promise of AI in Developing Economies | Global AI & Digital Summit
videos.description:
How can artificial intelligence create jobs and expand opportunities in developing economies? As AI reshapes economies and labor markets worldwide, countries face important choices about how to harness its potential while ensuring its benefits are broadly shared.

At the Global AI & Digital Summit in Seoul, World Bank Group Chief Economist Michael Kremer, Managing Director and Chief Knowledge Officer Paschal Donohoe, government leaders, and entrepreneurs discuss how AI can support economic development and job creation, and what governments and innovators can do to help close the digital divide. Michael Kremer was appointed Chief Economist and Senior Vice President for Development Economics in October 2026, while Paschal Donohoe serves as Managing Director and Chief Knowledge Officer.

videos.title: Small AI. Big Impact. | Global AI and Digital Summit
videos.description:
How can artificial intelligence create more and better jobs in developing economies? Explore how “small AI”—practical, locally adapted tools—can improve education, help farmers access markets, support small businesses, and strengthen public services.

Recorded at the Global AI & Digital Summit in Seoul, this discussion opens with World Bank Group President Ajay Banga on digital development, job creation, and moving AI from promising pilots to impact at scale.

Then, Bosun Tijani, Hoshik Shin, and Kate Kallot share examples from Nigeria, Tridge, and Amini. They examine what it takes to scale AI solutions: reliable local data, affordable connectivity, computing power, skills, investment, and procurement systems that enable local innovators to compete.

videos.title: The Race To Power AI Is Reshaping America's Electric Grid
videos.description:
AI data centers are driving unprecedented demand for electricity and putting renewed pressure on America’s power grid to modernize its equipment and develop greener, more efficient sources of power. Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon are all spending millions of dollars on local infrastructure upgrades and companies like SpaceXAI are even building off-grid power plants to power their data centers.

Google says its planned 780-megawatt data center in Pine Island, Minnesota, could offer a model for powering the AI boom. In a proposed agreement with Xcel Energy, Google says it will support 1,900 megawatts of new wind, solar and battery capacity, while minimum payments and exit fees are intended to protect local ratepayers if demand falls short.

CNBC examines whether projects like Pine Island can make the grid cleaner without shifting costs to existing customers, why some energy experts argue that smaller data centers could make better use of infrastructure already in place, and how utilities’ financial incentives can complicate efforts to build less.

videos.title: Why More Americans Regret College And Homeownership
videos.description:
For generations, mortgages and student loans have been held up as textbook examples of “good debt,".This borrowing promises to  build wealth or increase your earning power over time. On the other side of the coin is so-called “bad debt”, things like auto loans or credit card debt that don’t provide a financial return over time. As the costs of buying a home and getting a degree have continued to climb, more Americans are questioning whether those “good debt” investments are actually paying off.

videos.title: The Tiny Robot Solving a Massive Underground Crisis | WSJ
videos.description:
In January, a collapsed sewer pipe outside Washington, D.C., spilled more than 240 million gallons of raw sewage into the Potomac River. It is likely the largest sewage spill in U.S. history, but just one of an estimated 75,000 across the country each year, according to the EPA.

As aging sewer networks struggle with growing populations and changing weather patterns, a team of engineers and professors in Europe is developing a robot designed to detect and potentially address problems before disaster strikes.

WSJ explains how the $9 million EU-funded PIPEON project is tackling the dark and perilous world beneath our streets.

videos.title: Why There’s An ‘Extremely Fierce’ Battle For TSMC's Limited Chip Manufacturing Capacity
videos.description:
Unstoppable demand for AI is leading to a capacity crunch on factory lines at the world's leading chip manufacturer, Taiwan Semiconductor. And it could put a chokehold on AI's ability to scale. Analysts tell CNBC that Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom, AMD and others are locked in an “extremely fierce” competition to get their GPUs, CPUs and custom AI chips made at TSMC. Capacity can’t come online fast enough, despite TSMC’s rush to build new fabs in Taiwan, Japan and Arizona, where has expanded investment to $265 billion. The strain has made one man at TSMC “the most popular person on the planet,” as chip start-ups and big name CEOs visit Taiwan to ask him for wafer allocation. It’s also created a rich opportunity for Intel, as customers look to the long-struggling foundry arm of the U.S. chip manufacturer for a second source.

videos.title: How Cheap Mortgages Are Backfiring On Homeowners
videos.description:
Many Americans took advantage of historically low mortgage rates during the pandemic. But for homeowners who opted for adjustable-rate mortgages, those savings might not last. As mortgage rates continue to remain elevated, hundreds of thousands of borrowers are soon nearing the end of their introductory fixed-rate periods, putting them at risk of higher monthly payments. And with refinancing no longer offering the same relief it once did, some homeowners could find themselves facing a difficult financial decision.

videos.title: Why Retailers Are Shrinking Their Assortments
videos.description:
From Dollar General to Under Armour, retailers are culling assortments to get back to healthy growth, or at least, stabilize their business. For brands, excess inventory usually leads to discounting, which in turn hurts profitability. For box stores, slicing merchandise is more of a defensive play that allows for better curation. Watch the video to learn about why some retailers are giving consumers less choice.

videos.description:

Hy Luu, a 29-year-old Tesla investor based in Houston, offers a window into the rise in leverage after using six figures of margin and refinancing his home to reduce the risk of a margin call. CNBC's Sean Conlon explores what’s driving the rise in margin debt and what can happen when prices fall.

videos.title: The Megadonors Funding The 2026 Midterms
videos.description:
Billions of dollars have been raised for this year’s midterms elections, with a significant portion coming from big name tech billionaires in the cryptocurrency, artificial intelligence and online gambling sectors. Megadonors' contributions are overwhelmingly behind Republicans in the 2026 midterm election, with 14 of the 20 largest donor groups exclusively or nearly exclusively backing GOP candidates or outside groups. CNBC’s Luke Fountain reports.
